messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisa, a 31-year-old divorced paramedic of European background, came to treatment months after an assault that had occurred on duty and left her feeling as though her own body and mind had become unreliable witnesses. During a late-night call, she and her partner were met by police at the scene of a disturbance, and in the confusion of uniforms, shouted commands, and hands grabbing at her while she was trying to move a patient, one officer turned his aggression toward her. What happened next never settled into a clean sequence for her. When she tried to tell the story, she lost the thread halfway through and could not finish, circling back to fragments—a shove, the sting of being grabbed before she was ready, the metallic nausea that rose in her throat, a flash of a face in uniform—without being able to place them in order. She said the memory did not feel like something in the past at all; it came back with the force of something still happening, and that sense of immediacy made even ordinary reminders feel dangerous. A sudden touch from behind in the ambulance bay, a hand on her shoulder from a coworker, or the smell of stale sweat and adrenaline on a stressful shift could pull her back into that night so quickly that she would go pale and nauseated before she had time to think.

What frightened Marisa most was not only the memory itself but the feeling that it could erupt without warning into the present. Because the event remained so disorganized in her mind, she was left with a constant sense that danger might be hiding in the next moment, especially when she was around anyone in authority or in uniform. She began to watch people before they reached her, stiffening whenever someone moved too close, and she reacted with clear alarm when touched unexpectedly, even by a familiar colleague. At work she started choosing her seat obsessively, always looking for the place that felt most protected—against a wall, near an exit, never with her back exposed. She found herself scanning the station, the hospital corridors, and the back of the ambulance for signs of threat, her attention pulled to badges, posture, and the tone of a voice before she could focus on anything else. The more vividly the memory broke through, the more convinced she became that she had to stay on guard, and that vigilance began to spill into almost every part of her day.

Marisa coped by trying to keep herself tightly controlled. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to feel anger about what had happened, it would spill out and make her vulnerable or unprofessional, so she never allowed herself to feel or express it. She avoided anything that reminded her of the person who had harmed her, including assignments that brought her near police vehicles or scenes involving officers, and she tried to keep distance from authority figures whenever she could. These efforts brought some short-lived relief, but they also kept the event sealed off in a way that made it harder to sort out. When she tried to speak about it, she became even more tangled, as though holding herself back from anger and from the offending reminders stripped her of words as well as emotion. The more she pushed the material away, the more blurred and incomplete it became, and the more she doubted her own account of what had happened.

Over time, the cycle narrowed her world. Stress on shift became a trigger in itself, because tense calls, raised voices, and urgent decisions made her body feel ready for another sudden violation. Nausea would rise before she could name why, and that physical warning would send her back into scanning and seating herself in the safest possible place, while also making her work around officers and other authority figures feel increasingly intolerable. She avoided some scenes altogether when she could, traded tasks with coworkers, and kept conversations brief, especially if they touched on the assault. At home, after her divorce, the apartment grew quieter and smaller around her habits of vigilance, and she noticed that her whole day seemed organized around not being caught off guard. By the time she sought help, Marisa was exhausted by how much effort it took to keep herself contained and alert. She said she was finally coming in because she could not keep living as if every touch, every uniform, and every surge of stress meant she was about to be attacked again, and what she most hoped for was to be able to remember what happened without losing herself in it.
